text: Amazon EC2 is AWS's core compute service — a virtual server you rent by the second, the same idea as the Azure virtual machines you already know, built on AWS's own mechanics. Every launch, whether through the console or the CLI, boils down to the same five decisions: which AMI to boot from, which instance type, which network, how much storage, and how you'll get in.

A complete aws ec2 run-instances call makes those five decisions explicit as flags. --image-id and --instance-type are required on every single call — AWS needs to know the operating system and the hardware profile no matter how small the launch is. --subnet-id places the instance's network interface inside a specific VPC subnet instead of AWS guessing. --key-name and --security-group-ids determine how you'll authenticate into the instance and exactly what traffic is allowed to reach it once it's running.

Those five decisions never change, no matter how simple or complex the launch is. The AMI supplies the operating system and any software already baked in. The instance type sets the CPU, memory, and network performance available to the instance. The network decision picks the VPC and subnet it lives in. Storage sets the size and type of the root EBS volume. And the key pair plus security group decide how you log in, and what's allowed through the firewall.

The network decision has real consequences before the instance even boots. A subnet is public specifically because its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 traffic to an internet gateway — launch there with auto-assign public IP enabled, and the instance is reachable the moment it starts running. A private subnet has no such route, so there's no direct path in or out by design — exactly the right choice for an internal application server that should never be dialed into directly from outside AWS.

Once you can read a run-instances call by intent instead of copying it blindly, you're ready for the next piece of the puzzle: where that AMI actually comes from, and what happens to an instance as it moves from pending to running to stopped or terminated.
